extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged British readers, reformers, statesmen, and general public interested in government reform
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical/polemical essay arguing how national governments (especially Britain) should recruit and organise talent — selecting leaders by merit from all social ranks and reforming central administration (Downing Street) to serve living interests. It gives normative criteria for what good government and selection of statesmen should look like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose able men from whatever rank they are found
rubrics_metrics.description: “That the able man be chosen, in whatever rank be is found?” — able men should be searched for and chosen regardless of social class or birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search society like hidden treasure; train, supervise and set the able man to the work only he is fit for. The able poor (example: Robert Burns) often lack routes into Parliament or administration; institutions should be arranged to locate and promote such talent instead of relying on limited electorates or class-bias (e.g. Tenpound Constituencies, 'force of beer').

rubrics_metrics.name: Make parliamentary seat an ultimate, not primary, investiture
rubrics_metrics.description: “Make it ultimate instead of primary, a last investiture instead of a first indispensable condition” — the fact of sitting in Parliament should be the culmination of selection, not the prerequisite for public office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose leaders from the whole population (millions), not only from those already inside Parliament or from narrow constituencies; broaden the pool so the genuinely gifted can be chosen even if they did not first become MPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime Minister as a 'Reforming Premier' with authority to choose talent
rubrics_metrics.description: A true reforming statesman (Prime Minister) must be a ‘seeing’ noble person empowered to choose fitting subordinates from across the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give such a Premier latitude to select the fittest men from the whole population (under penalties if he neglects duty). This can be trialled safely in ways that an extension of the suffrage cannot; a single capable reforming Premier might achieve in ten years more than many Parliaments could.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's real aim: attain government by the Best (a truer Aristocracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy should be the method by which the able are sought out and placed into governance — 'the attainment of a truer and truer Aristocracy, or Government again by the Best.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ballot-boxes and suffrage movements are valuable only insofar as they help secure genuinely able men for governing tasks; democracy's essence is merit-based selection, not mere counting of heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments must recruit heroic intellect rather than mechanical or cunning talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments need 'heroic' (noble, high) intellects, not merely mechanical ('beaver') intellect or cunning ('vulpine'/'attorneyism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mechanical, money-seeking or merely technical intellect will not suffice for the higher task of guiding nations; neglecting noble intellect leads to decay, sham-wisdom and eventual anarchy. Thus selection should favor nobility of mind and heroic wisdom over mere administrative cleverness or rhetorical toughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: State institutions must provide routes of promotion for noble souls regardless of birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (historically the Church, convents, priesthood) should offer education, training and a career route so that gifted individuals from the lowest strata can rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one question in such systems was whether 'there is some human nobleness in you'; no inquiry about birth or capital. Modern polity should recreate institutions that function as 'lungs' — pervasive channels across society that admit and elevate the genuinely gifted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's role extends beyond 'keeping the peace' to managing living interests and removing dead ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should not be content merely to keep the peace; it must take on higher tasks of managing the nation's living economic and social interests and extinguishing obsolete, 'dead' interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A passive government that only maintains order neglects necessary active administration. The reform of central administration (Downing Street) should centre on directing energies to living interests and burning up extinct imaginary interests that encumber national life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate a nation's condition by the character of its governors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Tell me what kind of man governs a People, you tell me... what the net sum-total of social worth in that People has for some time been.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nature of those who govern (noble vs ignoble, beaver vs heroic intellect) reveals the nation's values and long-term prospects; this should be used as a diagnostic of social health and policy direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform central administration (Downing Street) to be staffed by gifted intellects
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'New Downing Street' should be inhabited by the gifted intellects of the nation directing energies to real interests and eliminating outdated institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a radical, slow and difficult reform requiring successive architects and builders; editors and unprofessional interference should be limited while the outlines of a new state architecture are drawn and implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of universal suffrage as the sole mechanism for selecting wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the suffrage to universal head-counting may produce sham-wisdom and 'Parliaments of the Paris pattern' that dissolve into eloquent but ineffective slush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal suffrage can be dangerous if it becomes merely counting heads without mechanisms to ensure noble or wise selection; alternative or supplementary methods (e.g., empowered reforming leaders tasked to recruit talent) should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test selection methods incrementally rather than relying on wholesale suffrage expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: “You could try this method with safety; extension of the suffrage you cannot so try.” — prefer experimentally empowering a capable executive to choose talent before widening franchise-based selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting an approximately heroic Prime Minister constrained but significant power to choose from the whole populace is a safer way to trial meritocratic selection than immediate, universal suffrage expansions which may have irreversible effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must themselves be noble and capable of recognizing nobleness in others
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ignobleness cannot, by the nature of it, choose the noble:... there needs a seeing man who is himself noble, cognizant by internal experience of the symptoms of nobleness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of officials depends on having leaders with internal experience of nobleness who can discern genuine ability in others; systems that allow ignoble selectors to dominate will fail to recruit true talent.
